The Magnetic Coulomb’s Law

§28.2–28.4 took the field as given. Ørsted’s needle says currents make it. Biot and Savart measured the field of each short piece of a current, and the result has the shape of Coulomb’s law for a piece of charge (Chapter 22). A current element \(I\,d\vec\ell\) makes, at a point a distance \(r\) away in the direction \(\hat r\),

\[\boxed{\;d\vec B = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\frac{I\,d\vec\ell\times\hat r}{r^2}\;}\]

where \(\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}\) is the permeability of free space from Chapter 31. Like Coulomb’s law, it is read from experiment, and the total field is the sum \(\vec B = \int d\vec B\) over the whole current.

Coulomb (Ch 22) Biot–Savart (this chapter)
Source charge \(dq\) current element \(I\,d\vec\ell\)
Field \(d\vec E = k\,\dfrac{dq}{r^2}\,\hat r\) \(d\vec B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,d\vec\ell\times\hat r}{r^2}\)
Falls off as \(1/r^2\) \(1/r^2\)
Direction along \(\hat r\), away from the source perpendicular to both \(d\vec\ell\) and \(\hat r\)

The last row is why \(\vec E\) points away from a charge while \(\vec B\) circles a current.

The Field of a Long Straight Wire

The calculation is the one Chapter 22 used for the field beside a charged rod, with the cross product in place of the components.

Step 1 — set up. Put the wire along the \(y\)-axis carrying \(I\) upward, and the field point \(P\) a distance \(a\) to its right (Figure 28.9b). An element \(dy\) at height \(y\) is a distance \(r = \sqrt{y^2 + a^2}\) from \(P\).

Step 2 — direction. For every element, \(d\vec\ell\times\hat r\) points the same way, into the page at \(P\), so the magnitudes simply add.

Step 3 — magnitude of one piece. \(|d\vec\ell\times\hat r| = dy\,\sin\phi\), where \(\phi\) is the angle between the wire and \(\hat r\), and \(\sin\phi = a/r\):

\[dB = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\,\frac{a\,dy}{(y^2 + a^2)^{3/2}}\]

Step 4 — integrate over the whole wire. With \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} dy/(y^2 + a^2)^{3/2} = 2/a^2\) (the same table integral as the charged rod),

\[B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\,a\cdot\frac{2}{a^2}\]

\[\boxed{\;B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\;}\]

writing \(r\) again for the distance from the wire. Direction: the field lines are circles around the wire. Point the right thumb along the current and the fingers curl the way \(\vec B\) goes (Figure 28.9a).

Check the result.

  • Far away. \(B \to 0\) as \(r \to \infty\), but only as \(1/r\), slower than a point source’s \(1/r^2\). It matches the infinite line of charge, \(E = \lambda/2\pi\varepsilon_0 r\) (Chapter 23): a long source falls off more slowly because there is always more of it nearby.
  • More current, more field. \(B \propto I\).
  • Units. \(\text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}\times\text{A}/\text{m} = \text{T}\).

The Field at the Center of a Loop

A loop of radius \(R\) is the easiest Biot–Savart sum of all, because every element is in the same position relative to the center (Figure 28.10).

Step 1 — geometry. Every element is a distance \(R\) from the center, and every \(d\vec\ell\) is perpendicular to the \(\hat r\) pointing at the center, so \(|d\vec\ell\times\hat r| = d\ell\).

Step 2 — direction. Every element’s field at the center points the same way, along the loop’s axis (the right-hand rule: fingers with the current, thumb along \(\vec B\) at the center).

Step 3 — add. The pieces add straight up to the loop’s length \(2\pi R\):

\[B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R^2}\oint d\ell = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R^2}(2\pi R)\]

\[\boxed{\;B_\text{center} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \qquad (N \text{ turns: } N\mu_0I/2R)\;}\]

Far from the loop along its axis the field falls off as \(1/x^3\), the same as the electric field far from an electric dipole (Chapter 22); this is stated, not derived here. A current loop is a magnetic dipole, the source of the \(\vec\mu\) of §28.4.

Example: A Coil and a Wire

(a) A flat coil of \(N\) turns and radius \(R\) carries current \(I\). Find the field at its center for \(N = 50\), \(R = 10.0\) cm, \(I = 2.00\) A, and compare it with Earth’s field. (b) Find the field \(10.0\) cm from a long wire carrying \(5.00\) A.

Why it matters: the current, the turns and the radius are all set on the bench; the field at the center is what the coil delivers. A pair of coils like this is how a laboratory makes a known field, or cancels Earth’s.

Step 1 — symbols.

\[B_\text{coil} = \frac{N\mu_0 I}{2R}, \qquad B_\text{wire} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\]

Step 2 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;B_\text{coil} = \frac{(50)(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.00)}{2(0.100)} = 0.628\ \text{mT} \approx 13\,B_\text{Earth}, \qquad B_\text{wire} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(5.00)}{2\pi(0.100)} = 10.0\ \mu\text{T}\;}\]

The modest coil overwhelms Earth’s \(50\ \mu\)T at its center. The wire’s field is a fifth of Earth’s at 10 cm and would equal it at 2 cm; this is why a compass held near a wire carrying a few amperes swings.

Two Wires: Superposition and the Force Between Currents

Magnetic fields add as vectors, just as electric fields did (Chapter 22). Two long parallel wires a distance \(d\) apart, with currents \(I_1\) and \(I_2\), each make the circular field of a single wire, and the field at any point is the vector sum. Run the right-hand rule once for each wire, then add (Figure 28.11a).

Each wire also sits in the other’s field and carries current across it, so each feels a force. Look at wire 2.

Step 1 — the field wire 1 makes at wire 2. A distance \(d\) away,

\[B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}\]

perpendicular to the plane of the wires.

Step 2 — the force on a length \(L\) of wire 2 (§28.3). The current \(I_2\) runs perpendicular to \(\vec B_1\):

\[F_{\text{on }2} = I_2LB_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1I_2L}{2\pi d}\]

Step 3 — direction. Both currents out of the page: wire 1’s field at wire 2 (on its right) points up the page, and \(I_2\vec L\times\vec B_1\) = (out) × (up) points toward wire 1. Parallel currents attract. Reverse \(I_2\) and the force reverses: antiparallel currents repel (Figure 28.11b).

Step 4 — the force on wire 1. Run the same steps with the labels swapped: \(F_{\text{on }1} = I_1LB_2 = I_1L\,\mu_0I_2/(2\pi d)\), the same size, pointing toward wire 2.

\[\boxed{\;\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d} \qquad \text{parallel currents attract, antiparallel repel}\;}\]

Check the result.

  • Newton’s third law, even with unequal currents. The formula is symmetric in \(I_1\) and \(I_2\): the force on wire 1 equals the force on wire 2 in size and is opposite in direction, however different the currents. A wire carrying ten times the current does not pull ten times harder; it makes ten times the field, which acts on the other wire’s smaller current.
  • One current turned off. As \(I_2 \to 0\), both forces go to zero together. Wire 1’s field at wire 2, \(\mu_0I_1/2\pi d\), does not change; there is simply no current in wire 2 for it to push on.
  • Far apart. \(d \to \infty\) gives \(F \to 0\), falling as \(1/d\).

This is where \(\mu_0\) comes from. Until 2019 the ampere was defined by this force: one ampere is the current that, in two long parallel wires one meter apart, gives a force of exactly \(2\times10^{-7}\) N per meter of wire. Put \(I_1 = I_2 = 1\) A and \(d = 1\) m into the result and it says \(\mu_0/2\pi = 2\times10^{-7}\), so \(\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\) T·m/A exactly. That is the “force between currents” Chapter 31 credited for the speed of light. (Since 2019 the ampere is fixed through the electron’s charge instead, and \(\mu_0\) is measured; it still agrees with \(4\pi\times10^{-7}\) to one part in \(10^{10}\).)

Example: Two Wires Carrying Opposite Currents

Two long parallel wires \(d\) apart carry \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) in opposite directions. Find the field at the midpoint and the force per unit length on each wire, for \(d = 10.0\) cm, \(I_1 = 3.00\) A and \(I_2 = 5.00\) A.

Why it matters: the currents and the spacing are set; the field between the wires and the force on them are what the design has to live with. In a power substation the busbars carry about 20 kA, 10 cm apart. The formula gives \(800\) N on every meter during a short circuit, and that is why the bars are bolted down.

Step 1 — the field at the midpoint. Each wire is \(d/2\) away. Seen end on, with \(I_1\) out of the page on the left and \(I_2\) into the page on the right, the right-hand rule gives both fields pointing up the page between the wires (Figure 28.11a), so the magnitudes add:

\[B_\text{mid} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi(d/2)} + \frac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi(d/2)} = \frac{\mu_0(I_1 + I_2)}{\pi d}\]

Step 2 — the force. From the result above, opposite currents repel:

\[\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}\]

Step 3 — numbers.

\[\boxed{\;B_\text{mid} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(3.00 + 5.00)}{\pi(0.100)} = 32.0\ \mu\text{T, up the page}\;}\] \[\boxed{\;\frac{F}{L} = \frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(3.00)(5.00)}{2\pi(0.100)} = 3.00\times10^{-5}\ \text{N/m, pushing the wires apart}\;}\]

The two wires feel the same \(30\ \mu\)N per meter, although one carries two-thirds more current than the other. With parallel currents the fields at the midpoint would oppose, giving \(8.0\ \mu\)T, and the wires would attract.
